Flags
flagz
n. pl. (reeds or rushes growing in shallow water; the growth among which the ark of bulrushes was laid and found)
Middle English flagge, a reed or rush — unrelated to the banner sense of the word, which is later. The Hebrew at Exodus 2:3 is suph, reeds — the same word in yam suph, the Sea of Reeds, which the Authorized Version renders the Red sea.

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew word is suph, and the coincidence of vocabulary is worth pausing over. Moses was hidden as an infant “in the flags by the river's brink” (Exodus 2:3), and found there when “she saw the ark among the flags” (Exodus 2:5). Eighty years later he would lead Israel through the yam suph, the sea of the same reeds. The infant drawn out of the water among the flags becomes the man through whom a nation is drawn out of the water. Isaiah uses the plant as a measure of judgment on Egypt's whole economy: “the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither” (Isaiah 19:6) — when the Nile fails, the marsh growth on which so much Egyptian life depended fails first. Bildad draws a proverb from the same botany: “Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11). His application to Job is wrong and unkind, but the observation is sound and Scripture uses it elsewhere rightly — what has no root in water withers when the sun is up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives flag as an aquatic plant, with long ensiform leaves, of several species — distinct from the banner sense of the word.

FLAG, n. An aquatic plant, with a bladed leaf, of the genus Iris; also a species of Acorus.

The flags of the Nile, among which the ark of Moses was laid.

FLAG, n. A cloth, usually bearing a device, borne on a staff; an ensign; a colors.

RUSH, n. A plant of the genus Juncus, growing in wet or moist ground.

BULRUSH, n. A large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water.

Key Scripture

Exodus 2:3 — "And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink."

Exodus 2:5 — "And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it."

Isaiah 19:6 — "And they shall turn the rivers far away; and the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither."

Job 8:11 — "Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?"

Modern Corruption

Exodus 2 is treated as a borrowed birth-legend, which removes the deliberate providence the narrative is constructed to display.

expand to see more

Critical treatments compare Exodus 2 to the Mesopotamian legend of Sargon, who was likewise set adrift in a reed basket, and conclude that the account of Moses is a literary borrowing meant to dignify a national founder. The parallel is real and proves nothing about historicity; exposed infants and river baskets were features of the ancient world, not of one story. What no parallel supplies is the structure Exodus builds: a decree that Hebrew sons be cast into the river, a mother who obeys the letter of it by placing her son in the river in a sealed ark, the daughter of the man who issued the decree drawing him out, and the child's own mother hired to nurse him at Pharaoh's expense. That is not legend-shape; it is providence-shape, and it is told with irony throughout.

The word ark in Exodus 2:3 is tebah, used elsewhere in Scripture only of Noah's ark — a vessel with no rudder, sealed with pitch, carrying the hope of a people through water that was killing everything else. The flags are the small physical detail that holds the whole scene together: they caught the ark, they kept it from the current, and they put it where Pharaoh's daughter would wash. Nothing in the account is presented as coincidence, and Hebrews 11 credits the parents' act to faith, adding that they were not afraid of the king's commandment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew suph, reeds or flags — Exodus 2:3, 2:5; the same word in yam suph, the sea of reeds; achu, marsh grass — Job 8:11; tebah, ark — Exodus 2:3.

expand to see more

Hebrew suph — reeds, flags; Exodus 2:3 and 2:5, and the yam suph Israel crossed.

Hebrew tebah — an ark or chest; used in Scripture only of Noah's vessel and Moses' basket.

Hebrew gome — papyrus, bulrush; the material of the ark itself.

Hebrew achu — marsh grass, meadow; Job 8:11, and the reed-grass of Pharaoh's dream.

Middle English flagge — a reed; unrelated to the later banner sense of the word.

Usage

"“She laid it in the flags by the river's brink” — the reeds that held the ark from the current."

"“When she saw the ark among the flags” — Pharaoh's daughter draws out Pharaoh's enemy."

"“Can the flag grow without water?” — Bildad's sound botany and unsound application."
